## What this is (and isn't)

One argument keeps coming up about the ฮั้ว ส.ว. (Senate collusion) case.
Several voters handed in identical ballots, the same names in the same
order, but defenders say a chance match isn't *impossible*, so collusion
can't be proven statistically. I wanted to see whether that holds up.

This piece doesn't try to decide the case, say who is guilty, or verify
the vote data myself. It does four narrower things:

1. Re-derives from scratch the probability figures that mathematician
   Loy Chunpongtong (ลอย ชุนพงษ์ทอง) published about the June 2024
   national-level Senate selection, to check the arithmetic.
2. Checks the method with a Monte Carlo simulation on a small version
   of the same problem.
3. Puts the result next to probability thresholds that science,
   forensics, and the courts already treat as conclusive. That
   comparison is the actual answer to "it's technically possible".
4. Uses simulated (not real) scores to show why a reported jump in vote
   totals between 6th and 7th place would point to bloc voting rather
   than noise.

Figures taken from news reports are linked in the Sources section at the
end. Anything I generated myself, like the simulations and the benchmark
table, is labelled as mine. Where the public data runs out, I say so.

## 1. Background

Thailand chose its Senate (สมาชิกวุฒิสภา) in June 2024 through a closed,
multi-round process. Candidates were split into 20 professional groups.
At the national round on 26 June, members of each group first voted
among themselves in the morning, cutting each group down to 40. In the
afternoon, groups voted across for each other's candidates to pick the
final 10 senators per group.

Since then, the Election Commission's inquiry, the DSI's AI-assisted
video analysis, documents released by opposition MPs, and
independent analysts have all pointed at the same accusation: blocs used
โพย (cheat-sheets) to coordinate their votes. That would leave a very
particular fingerprint, namely ballots with the same names in the same
order, filled in by people who say they don't know each other.

A senator from the accused side has said publicly that nothing unlawful
happened because no money changed hands, and that Thai courts have
previously ruled that bringing a cheat-sheet into the polling area isn't
a crime in itself. A separate defence, which I've seen repeated widely
but can't attribute to any specific senator, goes further: however
unlikely an accidental match is, it isn't *impossible*, so intent can't
be shown with statistics. That second claim is the one I'm testing.

## 2. The probability

The parameters come from public reporting. Each professional group at
national level had up to 154 candidates (77 provinces × 2). In the
morning round, each voter wrote up to 10 candidate numbers into ten boxes
on the ballot. Reports describe 10 ballots carrying the identical
sequence. If everyone voted honestly and independently, how likely is
that?

**A. Two ballots matching.** The number of ordered ways to write 10
different names out of 154 is the permutation count $P(154,10) =
154!/144!$. If voters pick uniformly at random, the chance that a second
ballot exactly copies a first one is one over that:

$$\frac{1}{P(154,10)} = \frac{1}{5.567 \times 10^{21}}$$

This is the same "1 in about 5,567 quintillion" figure Loy published. My
$\log_{10}$ of the denominator is 21.746, the same as his to three
decimals.

**B. All ten ballots matching.** Take ballot 1 as the reference. The
chance that ballots 2 through 10 each independently match it is that
number raised to the ninth power:

$$\frac{1}{P(154,10)^{9}} = \frac{1}{5.134 \times 10^{195}}$$

The denominator has 196 digits. For scale, the observable universe has
somewhere around $10^{82}$ atoms, which is smaller by a factor of about
$10^{114}$.

**C. Does the group size matter?** Not really. The smallest group
reported had 129 candidates, which is the most generous case for the
coincidence theory. That gives $P(129,10) \approx 8.92\times 10^{20}$, so a
two-ballot match is still about 1 in $10^{21}$.

**D. How small would the field need to be?** Smaller than it can get.
Even if there were only 10 candidates, so that every voter had to list
all of them, two ballots would only agree on the order 1 time in
$10! = 3{,}628{,}800$. A fifty-fifty chance of a match isn't reachable
with 10 ordered picks at any field size.

**E. What if voters aren't random?** This is the fairest objection.
Real voters don't pick uniformly: some candidates are better known, and
people from the same province may favour the same names. So suppose,
very generously, that every voter in the group ignored everyone except
the same 20 favourites and only had to decide the order. Two ballots
would still match only once in $P(20,10) \approx 6.7 \times 10^{11}$
tries, roughly 1 in 670 billion. Popularity can explain why the same
*names* turn up on many ballots. It can't explain the same names in the
same order, ten times over.

**In short:** two independent ballots matching by chance is about 1 in
$5.6\times10^{21}$, which agrees with Loy's figure. All ten matching is
about 1 in $5\times10^{195}$.

## 3. Checking the method

Numbers this large can't be checked by brute force, so I tested the
formula on a toy version I *could* simulate: 8 candidates, 3 picks.

| | value |
|---|---|
| Theoretical P(match), $n=8$, $k=3$ | 0.002976 |
| Empirical P(match), 300,000 simulated pairs | 0.002787 |
| Relative difference | 6.4% |

With 300,000 trials the standard error on that estimate is about 3.3%,
so the simulated value sits a little under two standard errors from the
formula. That's ordinary sampling noise, and nothing points to the
formula being wrong. The same formula applies at $n=154$, $k=10$; it just
can't be simulated there, since you'd need well over $10^{21}$ trials to
expect a single match.

Holding $k=10$ fixed and growing the field shows how fast the odds
collapse: about $10^{-6.6}$ at 10 candidates, $10^{-11.8}$ at 20,
$10^{-19.8}$ at 100, and $10^{-21.7}$ at the real figure of 154.

![Chance that two independent voters write the same ordered 10-name
ballot, by field size.](figures/fig1_probability_collapse.png){fig-alt="Line chart of log10 probability of an exact two-ballot match against number of candidates, falling from about -6.6 at 10 candidates to about -21.7 at 154."}

## 4. "It's not impossible"

The defence is that the match isn't literally impossible, so it could be
coincidence. That's true, but it doesn't help. Outside of logical
contradictions, nothing in probability is ever exactly impossible. If
"not exactly zero" were enough to dismiss evidence, no statistical
evidence could count for anything.

Here's where these numbers sit next to thresholds people already accept:

| scenario | log₁₀ probability |
|---|---|
| Statistical significance ($p<0.05$) | −1.30 |
| "Highly significant" in most sciences ($p<0.001$) | −3.00 |
| Being struck by lightning in a US lifetime (~1 in 15,300) | −4.18 |
| Six Sigma defect rate (~3.4 per million) | −5.47 |
| Winning a 6/49 lottery jackpot with one ticket | −7.15 |
| Random DNA profile match, unrelated person (common estimate) | −9.00 |
| Winning a 6/49 jackpot three draws in a row | −21.44 |
| **This case: 2 ballots matching by chance** | **−21.75** |
| Atoms in the observable universe, as a reference ($10^{82}$) | −82.00 |
| **This case: all 10 ballots matching** | **−195.71** |

*(The DNA and Six Sigma rows are standard order-of-magnitude reference
values, not figures from this case. They're there to show how unlikely
something has to be before courts and industry treat chance as ruled
out.)*

None of those rows is zero either. A drug trial with $p<0.05$ could
still be a fluke under the null hypothesis; we act on it anyway, because
calling it chance would be unreasonable. A DNA match at about one in a
billion isn't impossible, and courts still convict on it.

The two-ballot figure is about 13 orders of magnitude rarer than that DNA
match. The ten-ballot figure is about 114 orders of magnitude beyond the
number of atoms in the universe. And the "not impossible" argument works
exactly as well against odds of one in a billion as against odds of one
in $10^{195}$. An argument that never gets weaker however extreme the
numbers become isn't measuring anything. Whether something is possible
was never the right question. The right question is whether chance is
the best explanation, and here it clearly isn't.

## 5. A second pattern: the jump after 6th place

Separately from the matching ballots, Loy also pointed to the afternoon
round, where candidates ranked 1st to 6th in each group scored
unusually high compared with those ranked 7th to 10th. Under independent
voting you wouldn't expect a sharp break like that.

I don't have the real scores, so what follows is a **demonstration on
simulated data**, not a claim about the actual results:

| rank | independent voting | bloc voting |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 16.36 | 23.93 |
| 2 | 15.02 | 22.49 |
| 3 | 14.28 | 21.56 |
| 4 | 13.80 | 20.59 |
| 5 | 13.39 | 19.72 |
| 6 | 13.01 | 18.52 |
| 7 | 12.69 | 11.16 |
| 8 | 12.36 | 10.10 |
| 9 | 12.14 | 9.51 |
| 10 | 11.96 | 9.04 |

![Simulated average vote totals by rank across 200 simulated
elections, all 40 finalists shown. Illustrative only.](figures/fig3_score_distribution_simulation.png){fig-alt="Two lines of simulated vote totals by rank. Independent voting declines smoothly; bloc voting drops sharply between rank 6 and rank 7."}

The gap between 6th and 7th is **0.32 points** with independent voting
and **7.36 points** when a bloc votes together for a slate of six, about
23 times larger. Independent voting gives a smooth slope. A bloc gives a
cliff right where its slate ends, because its six candidates all get the
same block of extra votes and nobody else does.

That's the shape Loy described in the real data. This section only
shows *why* that shape would point to coordination if the description
is accurate. It doesn't confirm the real data looks like this or by how
much. It's a test to run once the actual tallies are public.

## 6. Summary

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Does the "1 in 5.567 × 10²¹" figure check out? | Yes. Re-derived independently; same number. |
| Is the method sound? | Yes. A small-scale Monte Carlo agrees within sampling error. |
| Does the exact group size matter? | No. The smallest reported group (129) still gives about 1 in 10²¹. |
| Does non-random voting rescue the coincidence theory? | No. Even limiting every voter to the same 20 favourites leaves odds of about 1 in 670 billion per pair. |
| Does "it's technically possible" work as a defence? | No. The same logic would throw out DNA evidence, clinical trials, and Six Sigma, none of which deal in zero probabilities either. |
| Does the reported jump after 6th place matter? | Probably, going by the simulation, but it needs the real vote data to confirm. |

Statistics can't settle intent. Who coordinated with whom, and whether
anything was paid or promised, are legal questions these numbers don't
answer. What they do show is that "the match is merely possible, so
chance can't be ruled out" doesn't survive contact with the standards of
evidence used everywhere else.
